points: System APIs: unlock data from systems of record (SAP, Salesforce, databases) and hide their complexity from everyone above.
Process APIs: combine and orchestrate data from several System APIs to carry out a business process, with no knowledge of the source systems or the channel.
Experience APIs: reshape data for one channel or consumer, such as a mobile app or a partner portal.
Application network: apps, data and devices connected through reusable APIs, so each new project reuses what the last one built.
C4E (Center for Enablement): a cross-functional team that publishes reusable assets, templates and best practices so teams can build their own APIs. It enables, it doesn't deliver every project.
principles: Reuse beats rebuild: a System API is built once and consumed by many Process APIs.
Change in one layer shouldn't ripple: swapping the CRM only touches its System API.

recall.q: Which API layer would you change when a mobile app needs a smaller response?
recall.a: The Experience API for that channel.

recall.q: What problem does the C4E solve that a central IT team doesn't?
recall.a: IT can't build everything; the C4E makes reusable assets and practices so line-of-business teams can build self-serve.

points: Design Center: where you write API specifications (API Designer) and turn on the mocking service.
Exchange: the catalog of reusable assets: API specs, RAML fragments, connectors, templates, examples and policies.
API Manager: manages API instances, applies policies, defines SLA tiers and approves client app contracts.
Runtime Manager: deploys Mule apps to CloudHub or your own servers, and sets their properties, workers or replicas.
Anypoint Monitoring: dashboards, metrics and logs for running apps.
Access Management: users, roles, business groups and environments (for example Sandbox and Production).
Anypoint Studio: the desktop IDE (Eclipse-based) for building Mule apps.

recall.q: You want to find a reusable Salesforce connector or an existing API spec. Where do you look?
Where do you apply a rate-limiting policy without redeploying the app?

points: GET: read a resource. POST: create one. PUT: replace one. PATCH: update part of one. DELETE: remove one.
2xx success: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content.
401 Unauthorized: missing or invalid credentials, for example no client_id with Client ID enforcement.
403 Forbidden: credentials are fine but access isn't allowed, for example an IP blocklist.
404 Not Found, 405 Method Not Allowed, 406 Not Acceptable, 415 Unsupported Media Type.
429 Too Many Requests: a rate limit or spike control policy was exceeded.
500 Internal Server Error: the default when a Mule flow fails and the error is propagated. 503 Service Unavailable: the service can't take requests right now.
Header: every RAML 1.0 file starts with #%RAML 1.0, then title, version and baseUri.
Resources: start with a slash (/flights) and can be nested (/flights/{ID}).
URI parameters: part of the path in braces, /flights/{ID}. In Mule they arrive in attributes.uriParams.ID.
Query parameters: declared under a method with queryParameters, ?airline=delta. In Mule they arrive in attributes.queryParams.airline.
Required by default: in RAML 1.0, parameters and properties are required unless you set required: false or add ? to the name.
Responses: keyed by status code, each with a body per media type, for example 200 > body > application/json > type and example.

recall.q: Write the RAML resource for one flight by ID.
In Mule, where does the value of ?airline=delta end up?

syllabusItem: RAML Types, Traits, Resource Types & Libraries
points: Data types: declared under types: and reused, e.g. Flight with properties; a ? suffix makes a property optional.
Traits: reusable method-level pieces (query params, headers, responses), applied with is: [pageable].
Resource types: reusable resource-level templates such as collection or member, applied with type: collection.
Libraries: a file of types, traits and resource types, imported with uses: and referenced with a prefix, e.g. lib.Flight.
Fragments: separate files with their own header (#%RAML 1.0 DataType, Trait, Library, NamedExample), pulled in with !include and shareable through Exchange.

recall.q: How do you apply a trait named pageable to a GET method?
How do you reference a type Flight from a library imported as lib?

points: Mocking service: in API Designer, it simulates the API from the spec and returns the example responses you defined, before any code exists.
Consumers can try the mock while the implementation is built in parallel.
Publishing: an API spec published from Design Center becomes a versioned Exchange asset (semantic versioning, e.g. 1.0.0).
Asset version vs API version: the asset uses major.minor.patch; the API's version field (e.g. v1) is part of the contract.
CloudHub 1.0: apps run on workers. You choose the worker size in vCores, the number of workers and the Mule runtime version.
CloudHub 1.0 app name: forms the public URL <app>.<region>.cloudhub.io, so it must be unique across CloudHub.
CloudHub 1.0 ports: the HTTP Listener should use ${http.port} (8081) or ${https.port} (8082); the load balancer forwards 80 and 443 to them.
CloudHub 2.0: apps run as replicas in shared spaces or private spaces; you choose replica count and size.
Runtime Manager properties: set at deployment and override the values in the app's property files.
Deploy routes: from Studio, by uploading the JAR in Runtime Manager, or with the Mule Maven plugin.
API instance: created in API Manager per environment; it has an API ID.
Autodiscovery: a global element in the Mule app with the API ID and a flowRef to the flow that has the HTTP Listener. The runtime pairs with API Manager and enforces its policies inside the app.
Autodiscovery credentials: the runtime connects with the environment's (org or business group) client ID and secret, not a consumer app's.
API proxy: API Manager generates a separate Mule app that sits in front of the implementation and enforces policies there.
When to proxy: the implementation isn't a Mule app, or you can't change and redeploy it.
Client ID Enforcement: requests must carry a registered client_id and client_secret; missing or wrong gives 401.
Rate Limiting: caps requests per time window for the API; over the limit gives 429.
Rate Limiting - SLA based: limits come from the caller's SLA tier, so it needs the client ID; over the limit gives 429.
Spike Control: smooths bursts by delaying or rejecting extra requests; rejected requests get 429.
SLA tiers: named limits (e.g. Gold 100/min) on an API instance, approved automatically or manually.
Client applications: a consumer requests access in Exchange, picks a tier, and gets a contract plus client ID and secret.
Policies are applied in API Manager without redeploying the app.
Property placeholders: ${db.host} in XML; p('db.host') in DataWeave.
Configuration properties: a global element points to a file, often per environment, e.g. config-${env}.yaml with env passed as a system property.
Secure Configuration Properties: a module that reads encrypted values, written in the file as ![encryptedValue].
Secure reference: ${secure::db.password} in XML and p('secure::db.password') in DataWeave.
The encryption key is passed at runtime (e.g. a -D system property), never stored in the project.
Hide in Runtime Manager: list sensitive property names under secureProperties in mule-artifact.json so their values are masked.
Global elements: connector configurations (HTTP Listener config, Database config) defined once and referenced by processors through config-ref.
Global elements in any XML file under src/main/mule are visible to flows in every other file of the same app; a common pattern is a global.xml.
src/main/mule: flow XML files.
src/main/resources: property files, .dwl modules, log4j2.xml, and API specs under api/.
src/test/munit: MUnit tests.
pom.xml: Maven dependencies (connectors, Exchange assets) and the Mule Maven plugin. mule-artifact.json: app descriptor, e.g. secureProperties.

syllabusItem: The Mule Event: Payload, Attributes & Variables
points: Mule event: a message plus variables. The message holds payload and attributes.
Payload: the main content, e.g. the HTTP request body.
Attributes: metadata from the source or the last operation, e.g. headers, queryParams, uriParams, method and requestPath from an HTTP Listener.
Variables (vars): values you set with Set Variable; they stay with the event through the flow and through Flow Reference calls.
HTTP Request without a target: replaces both payload (response body) and attributes (statusCode, headers, reasonPhrase). Vars survive.
Logger: reads the event but doesn't change it.

recall.q: After an HTTP Request without a target, what happened to payload, attributes and vars?
recall.a: Payload and attributes are replaced by the response; vars are unchanged.

points: Expression syntax: a field value wrapped in #[ ] is evaluated as DataWeave, e.g. #[payload.name].
Mule 4 uses DataWeave as its only expression language; Mule 3's MEL is gone.
Concatenation: ++ joins strings or arrays, e.g. #["Hello " ++ payload.name].
Interpolation: $( ) inside a string, e.g. #["Hello $(payload.name)"].
Default: payload.discount default 0 gives 0 when the value is null.
target: on an operation, stores its result in a variable instead of overwriting the payload.
With a target, payload and attributes stay as they were before the operation.
targetValue: what gets stored. Default #[payload] (the operation's output); #[message] stores payload and attributes; #[attributes.statusCode] stores just the status.
Use it to enrich: call a service, keep the result in a var, merge it into the original payload later.
Scaffolding: APIkit reads the RAML and generates a main flow, a console flow, and one flow per resource and method.
Main flow: HTTP Listener on /api/* followed by the APIkit Router, which validates the request against the spec and routes it.
Flow names: method:\resource:config, e.g. get:\flights:api-config and get:\flights\(ID):api-config. Methods with a body add the media type: post:\flights:application\json:api-config.
Error mapping in the main flow: APIKIT:BAD_REQUEST 400, NOT_FOUND 404, METHOD_NOT_ALLOWED 405, NOT_ACCEPTABLE 406, UNSUPPORTED_MEDIA_TYPE 415, NOT_IMPLEMENTED 501.
Status codes: the scaffolded handlers set vars.httpStatus, and the listener's responses use it.
Regenerating after a spec change adds flows for new resources and keeps existing ones.

recall.q: Which flow handles GET /api/flights/LAX if the RAML has /flights/{ID}?

syllabusItem: HTTP Listener: Building Interfaces by Hand
points: Listener config: host (0.0.0.0 to accept from any interface), port, and an optional base path shared by all listeners using it.
Listener path: can contain URI parameters, /flights/{dest}, available as attributes.uriParams.dest; /* matches anything below.
Allowed methods: restrict a listener to e.g. GET or POST.
Response and error response: set status code and headers, e.g. statusCode #[vars.httpStatus default 200].
Without APIkit, nothing validates the request against a spec; you check parameters yourself, e.g. with the Validation module.
Flow: an optional event source, processors, and its own error handling.
Private flow: a flow with no event source. It's called with Flow Reference and still has its own error handler.
Subflow: no event source and no error handler. It runs in the caller's context, so its errors go to the caller's handler.
Flow Reference: calls a flow or subflow synchronously with the same event. Changes to payload and vars in the called flow are visible to the caller afterwards.

recall.q: Which of flow, private flow and subflow can't have an error handler?

points: Flow Reference: an in-memory, synchronous call that passes the whole event, vars included.
VM connector: queues inside the app. Publish (fire and forget), Publish Consume (send and wait for the reply), Consume (read one message), and a Listener on the queue.
Across a VM queue the listener flow gets a new event: the payload (and attributes) travel, vars don't.
Queue types: transient (in memory, faster, lost on restart) or persistent (survives restarts).
On CloudHub 1.0 with persistent queues, VM messages can be picked up by any worker, which spreads load.

recall.q: Do variables cross a VM queue?
recall.a: No. Only the message goes; the listener flow starts a new event.

points: pom.xml: every connector and module the app uses is a Maven dependency there; adding one in Studio updates it.
Exchange assets (API specs, fragments, connectors) are pulled as Maven dependencies; the groupId is the organization ID.
Mule Maven plugin: builds the deployable JAR (mvn clean package) and can deploy it to CloudHub.
A missing or unreachable dependency fails the build; check the pom and repository credentials first.
